target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove work-schedule barriers for millions of voters and boost turnout by giving them time off
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off, so many private-sector workers—especially low-income retail and service workers—would still have to work or lose pay. Therefore, the holiday would not reliably remove the work-schedule barrier for the people most affected.

target: AG1's claim that an Election Day holiday would elevate civic participation and thereby increase democratic engagement
objection: Even if a holiday symbolically celebrates voting, the opponent argues that the motivational effect is not enough on its own to overcome the practical barriers many workers face, so the holiday's civic-salience effect would not reliably translate into higher turnout.

target: AG1's proposal as the best voting-access reform
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is unlikely to deliver large turnout gains on its own.

target: AG1's implication that a federal holiday is preferable to or sufficient alongside other reforms
objection: State-level measures requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to improve access than simply making Election Day a holiday.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday removes scheduling barriers because workplaces and schools will generally be closed
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee actual closure or usable time off for workers and school/daycare-related care arrangements, so the scheduling barriers may still remain for many voters.

target: AG1's claim that adopting a federal holiday would not delay other reforms because states can still act
objection: A high-profile national holiday can crowd out or reduce momentum for additional state-level reforms by making it seem like the problem has already been addressed, which can slow enactment of more targeted measures.

target: AG1's reliance on broad public support for the holiday as evidence it will not interfere with other reforms
objection: Broad support for a holiday does not imply similar support for the more burdensome reforms states would still need, so the holiday may actually weaken incentives to pursue those follow-on reforms.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would merely complement state reforms rather than undermine them
objection: Once Election Day is already a national holiday, employers and lawmakers can argue that further employer time-off or similar state reforms are redundant, which can strengthen resistance to and delay those reforms.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday's civic-salience benefits will support further reform rather than reduce it
objection: If the holiday itself produces only limited turnout improvements and does not require paid leave, it may reduce policymakers' urgency to pursue more effective reforms, thereby slowing future voting-access changes.
